own_scenes.desc: Una simulación repetitiva de la crudeza del funk negro, alargada por máquinas y no por músicos que improvisan. Nació en clubes europeos de finales de los sesenta que pinchaban funk original, llegó a Estados Unidos y en 1974 era la moda de la Costa Este: aceleró la destrucción de la sesión en directo, de las bandas y de la grabación con alma, y la música negra se volvió más mecánica y menos significativa. El disco quería bailar sin fin sobre un ritmo único; el funk, levantarse y hacer jam («Freak of the Week»: nada de ese «disco sádico» de un solo golpe). Las bandas de funk lo atacaron («The Undisco Kidd», «Anti-Disco» de Mutiny) o se vendieron: James Brown se proclamó «Original Disco Man», los Ohio Players, los Isley y Earth, Wind & Fire («Boogie Wonderland») cayeron. El grito «Disco sucks» metió en el mismo saco a toda la música negra de baile, y muchas bandas de funk murieron por no vender como el disco.

notes.text: En la era Carter, con Watergate, la crisis del petróleo y Nueva York en quiebra, el entretenimiento escapista pasó al centro de la cultura y la música «ciega al color» dio la impresión de una sociedad sin razas. Tras «The Hustle» de Van McCoy (1975) llegaron los clubes de pasos fáciles, el maxisingle de doce pulgadas, el poliéster y la cocaína; Saturday Night Fever (1978) vendió treinta millones y resucitó a los Bee Gees, Tavares y Kool & the Gang. El disco explotó la tradición negra de forma selectiva y racista: el «maratón de orgasmos» de «Love to Love You Baby» de Donna Summer y Giorgio Moroder (que Jesse Jackson y Operation PUSH quisieron boicotear) acabó con el arte negro de la insinuación. Tomó del funk la percusión africana, las cuerdas (Barry White y su Love Unlimited Orchestra) y los temas largos que había inventado James Brown, pero con máquinas: canciones sin principio ni catarsis, divas intercambiables (Anita Ward, Cheryl Lynn, Gloria Gaynor, Sister Sledge, Linda Clifford) y blancos en las listas de soul (KC and the Sunshine Band, Bee Gees, Village People, «Miss You» de los Stones). Hasta los auténticos cedieron: «Boogie Wonderland» de EWF, «It’s a Disco Night» de los Isley, «Party People» de Parliament, Masterjam de Rufus.

refs.q: Disco is the simplified form of nonethnic, electronic-sounding dance music that swept the country in the mid- to late 1970s.
refs.para: Disco is the simplified form of nonethnic, electronic-sounding dance music that swept the country in the mid- to late 1970s. The essence of disco is a repetitive simulation of the rawness of black funk, with music extended by machines and not by grooving, improvising musicians. Disco dancing was popularized in clubs in Europe in the late 1960s, playing records of black dance music—the original funk tracks. It later spread to the United States and by 1974 was the hottest dance trend on the East Coast. The mechanical aspects of disco music production swept the popular music industry, and accelerated the destruction of the live recording session, live bands, and the soulful recording experience. As a result, black music in general became less soulful, more mechanical, and less meaningful. While the ideals of disco were to dance interminably to monorhythmic beats, the ideals of funk were to get off your ass and jam. refs.q: The culture of disco exploited the black music experience in selective, manipulative, and ultimately racist ways.
refs.para: The culture of disco exploited the black music experience in selective, manipulative, and ultimately racist ways. When Donna Summer was “discovered” by producer Georgio Moroder, her sensuous, strong voice was exploited in ways never before heard of. Her novelty record “Love to Love You Baby” featured a fantastic simulated sex act “performed” by Summer that scorched the radio in early 1976. Her “marathon of orgasms” prompted a wide range of reactions, not the least of which was activist Jesse Jackson’s stand against what was being called “sex-rock.” Jackson and his Chicago-based Operation PUSH (People United to Save Humanity) threatened to boycott records and distributors associated with the “garbage and pollution which is corrupting the minds and morals of our youth.” PUSH sponsored a number of conferences on “X-rated” rock music, which included the denunciation of such gems as Johnnie Taylor’s “Disco Lady” and K.C. and the Sunshine Band’s “Shake Your Booty.”

refs.q: The long-playing dance single was an innovation that should be credited to James Brown.
refs.para: The long-playing dance single was an innovation that should be credited to James Brown. His bands performed in the ageless African tradition of extended dance workouts, improvising along the simplest of patterns and filling up the space with lively rhythmic interplay. Brown’s courageous impulse to record his songs as long dance cuts—seven minutes of “Cold Sweat,” ten minutes of “Sex Machine,” thirteen minutes of “Papa Don’t Take No Mess”—were copied by funk bands initially, and then by disco producers who used machines instead of bands to extend their songs.

refs.q: Universal Funk gave way to color-blind, brain-dead pop.
refs.para: Universal Funk gave way to color-blind, brain-dead pop. Initially, there had been stiff criteria for white performers to succeed in black music, but disco changed that. The heavy funk of the Average White Band gave way to the lightweight, grooving dance funk of K.C. and the Sunshine Band, which opened the doors for the Australian trio the Bee Gees, the gay macho spoof of the Village People, the biggest-selling black chart hit of the Rolling Stones (“Miss You” in 1978), and finally the easy-rock duo Captain & Tennille’s ironic “Do That to Me One More Time,” in 1980. For the first time since the heyday of Elvis Presley in 1960, white groups made steady inroads onto the black charts, and not everyone was thrilled about it. own_scenes.desc: Al subir el bombo y las líneas de bajo del funk y el soul, la música libera su componente hedonista: hacer bailar en las discotecas y elevar el voltaje erótico del sonido.

notes.chapter: Cap. 5: Poderosamente real: la música disco, de The Loft al Paradise Garage (1970-1985)
notes.text: Más que un estilo, un fenómeno social de escapismo e hibridación: wasps, negros, gays e hispanos iguales en la pista. David Mancuso abre The Loft en 1970 (sound system a medida, sesiones como un continuum de emociones, primer record pool en 1975); Francis Grasso, en Sanctuary, es el primer DJ que mezcla dos discos de verdad. Meco Monardo sube bajo y batería en la mezcla de «Never Can Say Goodbye» de Gloria Gaynor: el primer hit de la era disco. Tom Moulton y José Rodríguez inventan por accidente el maxi-single de 12 pulgadas; Walter Gibbons lo estrena comercialmente con «Ten Percent» (Salsoul, 1976). Studio 54 (1977-1980) es el epicentro; la Disco Demolition Night de Chicago (1979) y su cierre, el final.

notes.chapter: Loops 2 · Epílogo: Postales desde el «no lugar»: sueños utópicos de la música de baile
notes.text: La disco y el primer house como teología de la liberación: cuerpo y utopía, banda sonora de la liberación gay como el soul lo fue de los derechos civiles. «En cuanto mezclas a los distintos grupos económicos, empieza el progreso social» (David Mancuso, 2016).

refs.q: A principios de 1970 sus fiestas en su propio apartamento del bajo Broadway
refs.para: Si tratamos de pioneros, toca hablar indefectiblemente de David Mancuso. A principios de 1970 sus fiestas en su propio apartamento del bajo Broadway congregaban a una bulliciosa parroquia con ganas de divertirse hasta que el cuerpo aguantase. Lo que inicialmente había nacido como una ingeniosa manera de pagarse el alquiler de su espacio evolucionó rápidamente en meetings semanales a los que solo se podía acceder por invitación personal del propio Mancuso. Más cerca de una reunión de amigos que de un club al uso, The Loft fue un evento de carácter familiar, sin apenas gastos en decoración, donde el protagonismo recaía realmente en la gente, y los zumos y la fruta sustituían al alcohol. Este ambiente distendido disfrutó de una banda sonora a su medida, servida por el anfitrión en persona, un embriagador cóctel que incluía una abigarrada selección en la que tanto cabían los grandes himnos de un género en crecimiento («Love Is the Message», del colectivo de Filadelfia MFSB) como exóticos imports europeos, ya fueran el afrobeat de Manu Dibango o el funk de los españoles Barrabás. Por supuesto, también espirituales himnos soul: una música que ensalzó el sentimiento de comunidad de los que allí se citaban y de la que tomaron buena nota varios de sus habituales, unos jovencísimos Larry Levan, Frankie Knuckles o Tony Humphries, que ya desde aquellos tempranos días se dejaban caer por The Loft.
refs.chapter: Cap. 5: Poderosamente real: la música disco, de The Loft al Paradise Garage (1970-1985)

refs.q: al ser el primer DJ en mezclar efectivamente
refs.para: Pronto otros como Tee Scott o Mancuso se hicieron eco de la innovación. Sin embargo, Grasso les superó y fue más allá al ser el primer DJ en mezclar efectivamente —y perfectamente: los empalmes de Terry Noel unos años antes no pueden compararse— dos discos. «En aquellos días era imposible ajustar las velocidades. Tenías que atraparlo en el momento justo, no había espacio para el error. Tampoco podías acelerarlo para corregirlo, no podías tocar los platos... Todo lo que tenías que hacer era empezar en el momento justo. Nadie mezclaba como yo, ninguno se atrevía a dejarlos tanto rato, porque si lo hacías las posibilidades de error aumentaban. Para mí era algo natural, tan sencillo como pasear a mi perro», explicaba en Last Night a DJ Saved My Life. Francis Grasso marcó una transformación total en la figura del DJ. El auge de las discotecas había dado luz a un nuevo tipo de disc-jockey —prolongado por sus discípulos Steve D’Acquisto y Mchael Cappello—, alguien capaz de crear la atmósfera adecuada a través de la música.
refs.chapter: Cap. 5: Poderosamente real: la música disco, de The Loft al Paradise Garage (1970-1985)

refs.q: había nacido el primer hit de la era disco
refs.para: Aquella fue una idea nueva, hasta cierto punto revolucionaria, pero que no tardó en tener otras materializaciones. En 1974 el productor Meco Monardo contrató a la entonces desconocida cantante Gloria Gaynor para grabar un par de temas, «Honey Bee!» y «Never Can Say Goodbye». Hasta aquí nada de particular: no era más que una de las muchas sesiones que se sucedieron en los Media Sound Studios de Nueva York. Pero cuando llegó el momento de hacer la mezcla, Monardo tomó una decisión revolucionaria: en lugar de dejar la sección rítmica como acompañamiento —la práctica entonces más habitual— subió los canales del bajo y la batería y los colocó en primer plano, para así dejar atrás la orquesta y la voz de la cantante. El resultado fue sorprendente: había nacido el primer hit de la era disco. Obviamente, pronto surgieron otras producciones que intentaron imitar el éxito de «Never Can Say Goodbye», como el intento de Mchael Kunze, que se encerró en el estudio con tres vocalistas y un bajista para obtener como resultado «Fly, Robin, Fly», conocido en la industria como «el milagro de Monaco». Era un tema sencillo: tan solo una fantástica sucesión de bajos sobre los que The Silver Convention ejercitaban sus piruetas vocales. El tema arrasó inmediatamente en las listas americanas.
refs.chapter: Cap. 5: Poderosamente real: la música disco, de The Loft al Paradise Garage (1970-1985)

refs.para: Fue este tándem el responsable de la aparición de uno de los inventos más radicales y que más impulsaron la emergente cultura de baile: el single de doce pulgadas. Según cuenta la leyenda, a Rodríguez se le habían acabado las placas de siete pulgadas. Moulton, que quería tener cuanto antes el acetato de «I’ll Be Holding On», de Al Downing, le propuso plancharlo en una placa de diez pulgadas. «Parecía tan ridículo, aquella banda tan estrecha planchada en un disco grande...», recordaba Moulton en una de sus entrevistas. «Pensé qué pasaría si lo agrandábamos aún más... José contestó que debía subir el nivel hasta +6. Yo le dije que adelante.» Accidentalmente, había nacido el maxi-single. Este revolucionario formato permitía no solo una mayor duración de los temas, sino que ofrecía un volumen y calidad de sonido hasta entonces inauditos. Arthur Baker, el futuro productor que inventaría el electro, recuerda hoy la primera vez que vio un maxi-single. «Fui a ese club y había un tipo diminuto en la cabina que pinchaba stompings... Un tema me sonaba, pero no lo reconocía. Pinchaba un doce pulgadas... eso era raro. El disco era Ten Percent. Me afectó la percepción, fue increíble. Me abrió hacia muchas posibilidades sonoras, fue una revolución.» El club en cuestión era Galaxie 21 y el «tipo diminuto» su DJ residente, Walter Gibbons. Este era también el responsable de la explosiva mezcla del «Ten Percent» de Double Exposure que sonaba por los altavoces, el primer doce pulgadas comercializado por Salsoul.
refs.chapter: Cap. 5: Poderosamente real: la música disco, de The Loft al Paradise Garage (1970-1985)

refs.q: En 1977 abrió sus puertas en Nueva York la llamada
refs.para: En 1977 abrió sus puertas en Nueva York la llamada «reina de las discotecas», Studio 54. Durante los casi cuatro años en los que permaneció abierto, el club se convirtió en el epicentro del universo disco: el templo del baile y del desenfreno por antonomasia. Situado en pleno corazón de Manhattan, justo al lado de Broadway, en el 254 de la calle Cincuenta y cuatro Oeste, fue el resultado de la ambición de dos audaces vividores que respondían al nombre de Steve Rubel e Ian Schraeger. Con la ayuda de un tercer socio capitalista, el magnate del comercio Jack Dushey, convirtieron un antiguo teatro de los años veinte, el San Cario Opera House, en lo que muchos denominaron «la octava maravilla del mundo». En tan solo seis semanas la pareja Rubel-Schraeger ideó lo que quería ser el club más exclusivo y fascinante de todos los tiempos.
refs.chapter: Cap. 5: Poderosamente real: la música disco, de The Loft al Paradise Garage (1970-1985)

refs.q: colocaba el primer clavo en el ataúd del fenómeno disco
refs.para: Con la clausura de Studio 54 se dio por finalizada la locura disco. Es el punto y final de un proceso degenerativo que había tenido su primera manifestación importante un año atrás en la llamada Disco Demolition Night. El famoso evento en el Comiskey Park de Chicago, en el que cientos de fans del rock quemaron miles de discos al grito de Disco sucks! («la música disco apesta»), colocaba el primer clavo en el ataúd del fenómeno disco, que empezó a perder el favor popular.
refs.chapter: Cap. 5: Poderosamente real: la música disco, de The Loft al Paradise Garage (1970-1985)

refs.q: La capacidad de la música de baile de vehicular las esperanzas y deseos utópicos
refs.para: La capacidad de la música de baile de vehicular las esperanzas y deseos utópicos jamás ha sido tan evidente como lo fue en las pistas de baile de Estados Unidos durante las décadas de los setenta y los ochenta. La música disco aúna la inmediatez física del funk con los temas líricos del soul y el góspel; ritmos percutivos y líneas de bajo incitadoras que invocaban la presencia del cuerpo que bailaba en el aquí y ahora, mientras las melodías de cuerdas elevaban el espíritu y los estribillos corales transmitían la esperanza de un futuro, igual que los himnos góspel evocaban una vida mejor después de la muerte.[4] Pese a que los temas líricos explícitos no acostumbraban a ser religiosos ni políticos, sino con frecuencia románticos en el sentido convencional, sus cualidades optimistas y motivadoras siguen conmoviendo a muchos. Fue en parte una música con la cualidad de toda una teología de la liberación.

podcast.title: Coming of Age (1974-1975)
podcast.body: Disco music, characterized by lush club sounds, began its significant breakthrough on the charts around 1974 and 1975, signaling its maturity as a musical form. "Musically, it's signaled that disco had come of age."

podcast.title: Emergence in 1974
podcast.body: Disco music began its ascent in 1974, with chart successes like George McCrae's "Rock Your Baby" and Barry White's "Love's Theme" serving as indicators of its arrival.

srcs.episode: Ep. 48 - The Worst of the 70s The Music of 1974

podcast.title: First Billboard Disco Dance Chart (1974)
podcast.body: In late October 1974, Billboard began publishing a Disco Dance Chart, which was compiled based on reports from club DJs and mirrored Vince Letty's weekly disco column in Record World. "Billboard began publishing a disco dance chart, which was compiled based on whatever the DJs were reporting."

srcs.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)

podcast.title: Pre-Disco Era in 1974
podcast.body: In 1974, the full advent of the disco era had not yet occurred, placing ABBA's early pop sound outside of this burgeoning genre. "and we were not quite yet into the disco era in 1974."

srcs.episode: Ep. 56 - Talk Shows of the 1970s

podcast.title: "Four on the Floor" Dominance (1975)
podcast.body: In the second half of 1975, "four on the floor" dance music became increasingly prevalent on the radio, with multiple hits in this style charting between late summer and New Year's Eve. "In the second half of 1975, this four on the floor dance music was becoming more and more prevalent on the radio."

srcs.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)

podcast.title: 7-Inch Records for DJs (1975)
podcast.body: By 1975, record companies started producing 7-inch records specifically labeled "for disco DJs only," as this format was easier for DJs to work with. "Seven inch records that were labeled for disco DJs only were produced because they were easier for DJs to work with."

srcs.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)

podcast.title: Record Company Investment (1975)
podcast.body: By February 1975, record companies recognized the commercial potential of disco, beginning to issue remixes and extended LPs of club hits to capitalize on their popularity. "In February 1975, we can see that record companies are starting to capitalize on the club hits."

srcs.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)

podcast.title: Dilution and Saturation Concerns (1976)
podcast.body: A Tallahassee, Florida DJ commented in July 1976 that updating old standards like "Venus," "Volare," and "Strangers in the Night" with disco beats was monotonous and diluted disco's appeal, signaling "the road to saturation." "updating old standards like Venus, Volare, and Strangers in the Night with disco beats was monotonous."

srcs.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)

podcast.title: George Steinbrenner's Morale Boost (1976)
podcast.body: In 1976, New York Yankees owner George Steinbrenner ordered disco music to be played in the Yankees locker room as a means to lift team morale. "In 1976, New York Yankees owner, George Steinbrenner, ordered that disco music be pumped into the Yankees locker room to lift morale."

srcs.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)

podcast.title: Soho Newspaper Criticism (1976)
podcast.body: A Soho newspaper in New York, in May 1976, published an article condemning dance halls for attracting "truly evil people" and preying on community innocence, claiming these places had "nothing to do with either" dancing or music. "these dance halls have brought to this neighborhood the truly evil people who work New York."

srcs.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)

podcast.title: Vince Letty's Defense Against Bigotry (1976)
podcast.body: In May 1976, music journalist Vince Letty responded to criticisms of disco by citing a New York Post article that mentioned discos "reportedly attract substantial numbers of Blacks, Hispanics, and homosexuals." Letty urged the "party people" to assert their rights against the "bigotry sexism and hypocrisy" of communities criticizing disco. "If there is a disco community and I believe there is, Blacks, Hispanics, and homosexuals are at its core."

srcs.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)

podcast.title: Widespread Ubiquity (1976)
podcast.body: By 1976, disco had become ubiquitous across the United States, making it impossible to avoid on radio or in record stores, even for those who disliked it. "you could go to just about any part of the United States and find a disco in 1976 right on into the 1980s."

srcs.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)

podcast.title: Dominance in 1977
podcast.body: Disco became the "king" of both the dance floor and radio in 1977, dramatically sweeping over the music industry "like a tidal wave" and significantly impacting the visibility and success of other genres like reggae. "My theory on this is very simple disco disco was king not just on the dance floor, but on the radio in 1977 it came over the music industry like a title wave."

srcs.episode: Ep. 29 - Every Little Thing is Gonna Be All Right - The Influence of 70s Reggae

podcast.title: Dominance in Post-1977 Era
podcast.body: Following the punk and new wave era, disco, pop, and hair metal dominated a "long follow period," which, while popular, was not seen as music that changed the world. "lots of disco, lots of pop, lots of hair metal, which was great if you were into that kind of thing, but not exactly music that changed the world"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Amazing Year That Was 1991

podcast.title: Emergence from R&B (1977)
podcast.body: Disco emerged as a significant new genre from R&B in 1977, following a "big split" in musical styles. Its appearance led to considerable polarization but ultimately established an "incredible" and lasting legacy. "On the R&B side, we got disco."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 2: (90-81)

podcast.title: I Feel Love (1977) as Futuristic Disco
podcast.body: Donna Summer's "I Feel Love," produced by Giorgio Moroder in 1977, was a significant disco album, yet it distinguished itself with a "robotic, futuristic" sound. This innovative approach, driven by Moroder's experimentation with synthesizers, made it extremely inspirational for those exploring electronic music. "The album was disco, but it was different, robotic, futuristic, and those who were into experimenting with synths found it to be extremely inspirational."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Key Alt-Rock Movie Soundtracks

podcast.title: 1978-1982 Music Industry Revolution
podcast.body: Between 1978 and 1982, the music industry underwent a significant revolution, during which disco music experienced a rapid decline. This period was characterized by the emergence of new musical styles. "la música disco, la calle en picado"

srcs.episode: Cómo Michael Jackson hizo el disco más vendido de la historia

podcast.title: Peak Influence in 1978
podcast.body: By 1978, disco music had reached its peak, exerting a significant influence across the music industry. The Rolling Stones, for instance, incorporated disco elements into their "Some Girls" album. "la música disco ya estaba por todo lo alto."

srcs.episode: The Rolling Stones: Some Girls y su portada llena de demandas.

podcast.title: Polarizing Force (1978)
podcast.body: In 1978, disco was an intensely polarizing force in music, compelling fans to gravitate away from mainstream sounds and towards the expanding fringes of popular music. It was profoundly hated by rock fans, who condemned it as "evil, vacuous, boring, mindless, empty and obnoxious." "That repulsive force, that dark matter was known as disco."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 6

podcast.title: Anti-Disco Riots (1979)
podcast.body: In 1979, the anti-disco riots erupted in the United States, marking a significant downturn for the disco movement. Conservative groups publicly burned disco albums, leading to widespread censorship in many conservative regions. These events ultimately signaled the beginning of the end for disco and curtailed the careers of many prominent artists in the genre. "justo en 1979 se generan los estúrbios antidiscos cuando grupos conservadores empiezan a quemar públicamente álbumes de música disco y empieza a ver a una censura enorme en muchas partes son tanto conservadoras de Estados Unidos."

srcs.episode: Grace Jones - Inicios de la Disco Queen

podcast.title: Dominant in 1979
podcast.body: 1979 was a year "full of disco," which made The Knack's "My Sharona" (a rock song) an unexpected number one and a point of contention among rock fans. "Loathed for scoring Rock's first big number one in a year full of disco."

podcast.title: Late Disco Influence on Early Rap (1979)
podcast.body: Late disco music contributed significantly to the background sound of the first modern rap releases in 1979, alongside funk and boogie, before hip hop developed its own distinct musical identity. "recuerdan sobre todo al buggy y no tanto al hip hop hay un es como que entre el rap como una evolución dentro de lo que sería la música fankey de lo que sería el buggy del final de la música disco."

srcs.episode: El RAP antes del RAP (los primeros años del rap)

podcast.title: Transition from Rap (1979-1983)
podcast.body: Rap underwent a rapid evolution between 1979 and 1983, during which it separated itself from its late disco roots to establish the distinct musical foundations of hip hop. "acabaría separando el rap con esos restos era música buggy y era música disco tardía a lo que sería lo que serían las bases del hip hop."

srcs.episode: El RAP antes del RAP (los primeros años del rap)

podcast.title: Disco Backlash of 1980
podcast.body: In the early summer of 1980, the music business was actively contending with a significant disco backlash. Despite this, a string of hits emerged that seemed to defy conventional wisdom, being danceable and bathed in disco strings, yet also sophisticated, meticulous, brassy, and even jazzy, such as "Stomp" by The Brothers Johnson and "Off the Wall" by Michael Jackson. "44 years ago in the early summer of 1980 as the music business was contending with the disco backlash."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: I Wanna Rock with Q. Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Early Breakbeat Influence (1980)
podcast.body: While Kurtis Blow's "The Breaks" introduced breakbeat culture in 1980, it was still heavily influenced by disco music, showcasing the transitional phase of rap. "introduce la cultura del break beat pero todavía muy influenciado con el buggy con el disco."

srcs.episode: El RAP antes del RAP (los primeros años del rap)

podcast.title: Ebbing Popularity (1980)
podcast.body: By 1980, disco's popularity was ebbing, yet Blondie's "Call Me" showed how dance music could evolve and make a successful transition into the new decade. "Even as disco was ebbing in popularity, could make the transition into a new decade."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

srcs.episode: Hits of the Year Edition Part 2

podcast.title: Economic Downturn Contribution (1980)
podcast.body: The bursting of the disco bubble in 1980 contributed to a major recession in the recording industry, with sales dropping 10% year over year. This economic downturn, coupled with high interest rates, meant that people were less willing to spend discretionary income, making the industry ripe for a new marketing tool like music videos. "The disco bubble had burst."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Future of the Music Video - Part 1

podcast.title: "Four on the Floor" Beat Innovation
podcast.body: The signature "four on the floor" rhythm, which became the heartbeat of disco and defined the sound of the late 1970s, was pioneered by drummer Earl Young. He achieved this by skillfully using his kick drum and hi-hat to create a continuous, driving groove. "He used his kick drum and his hi-hat to make the four on the floor sound that really turns out to be the heartbeat of disco and then in many ways, the heartbeat of the late 70s."

srcs.episode: Ep. 50 - The Travolta Trilogy

podcast.title: "Rock Your Baby" as an Early Example
podcast.body: George McCray's 1974 song "Rock Your Baby" is identified as one of the very first disco records, marking an early significant entry into the genre. "now I want you to listen to the drum machine here in one of the first if not the first disco records rock your baby in 1974."

srcs.episode: FTR70 Sound Bite - Remembering Sly Stone

podcast.title: 1970s Criticism of Emptiness
podcast.body: In the 1970s, Disco music was heavily criticized as boring, repetitive, and devoid of content and musical creativity, particularly when compared to the funk music of James Brown or soul music. Despite this, it is now considered an integral part of music history. "cuando nacía la música disco en no 70 decían que eso evidentemente comparado con la música fanque de James Brown o la música soul en la música disco no era más que música aburrida repetitiva y vacía de contenido y vacía de creatividad musical."

srcs.episode: EL TRAP SÍ ES MÚSICA. (Aunque a lo mejor no te guste)

podcast.title: Affordability Driving Popularity
podcast.body: One reason for disco's widespread appeal was the rising cost of rock concerts, making discos a more affordable entertainment option for dancing. "going to rock concerts was getting too expensive."

srcs.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)

podcast.title: African Roots in Disco
podcast.body: Manu Dibango's 1972 track "Soul Makossa" is cited as clear evidence of the significant African roots within the burgeoning disco genre, gaining initial popularity through New York's club scene and DJs rather than traditional radio. "It is also clear evidence of the African roots in disco."

srcs.episode: Ep. 33 - Zaire '74, Muhammad Ali, and The Rumble in the Jungle

podcast.title: American Black Audience Preference (70s)
podcast.body: In the 1970s, American black audiences, the "most coveted" by Bob Marley, were heavily influenced by "elaborately costumed disco" and funk, which was seen as a factor in their disinterest in reggae. "They were under the sway of a elaborately costumed funk and disco and seemed determined to avoid any reminder of their own African roots, fearful of the stigma of primitivism."

srcs.episode: Ep. 29 - Every Little Thing is Gonna Be All Right - The Influence of 70s Reggae

podcast.title: Association with the 70s
podcast.body: Disco is a musical genre that is exceptionally and closely associated with the decade of the 1970s, more so than many other genres are with their respective decades. "there are not too many musical genres that are as closely associated with a decade as disco is with the 70s."

srcs.episode: FTR70 Sound Bite - Remembering Sly Stone

podcast.title: Bee Gees as "Poster Demons"
podcast.body: The Bee Gees, prominently associated with the *Saturday Night Fever* soundtrack, were demonized by rock fans. They were cast as the "people who destroyed music" due to their immense popularity and influence within the disco movement. "The Bee Gees, the people behind the Saturday Night Fever soundtrack, were poster demons as the people who destroyed music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 6

podcast.title: Billboard Chart Dominance in the 70s
podcast.body: Disco music ascended to prominence on the Billboard charts by the end of the 1970s, effectively replacing Bubblegum Music as a leading genre. This rise signified a major shift in mainstream musical taste. "it gave way on the Billboard charts to disco."

srcs.episode: Ep. 30 - The Sweet Sound of 70s Bubblegum Music
Ep. 30 - The Sweet Sound of 70s Bubblegum Music

podcast.title: Bowie's Influence and Crossover
podcast.body: David Bowie experimented with disco as one of his many styles. His song "Fame" in 1975 read as "De facto Disco" on Top 40 radio, crossing over to the Soul Singles Chart at a moment when disco was just breaking on the charts with hits by artists like the Bee Gees, Van McCoy, and KC and the Sunshine Band. "On top 40 Radio, Fame read as De facto Disco. At a moment when Disco was just breaking on the charts, in hits by the Bee Gees Van McCoy, and Casey and the Sunshine Band."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Starman to Blackstar Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Bubble Burst Impact (Early 1980s)
podcast.body: The bursting of the disco bubble at the dawn of the 1980s was a significant factor contributing to the record industry's first major sales crisis, as it caused record sales to go into "free fall." "At the dawn of the 80s, the disco bubble had burst and record sales were suddenly in free fall for the first time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1

podcast.title: Call for Destruction
podcast.body: Rock fans expressed an intense desire for disco to be "despised, shunned, mocked, sabotage and ultimately destroyed," highlighting the profound animosity and cultural divide that the genre created. "disco was evil, vacuous, boring, mindless, empty and obnoxious and needed to be despised, shunned, mocked, sabotage and ultimately destroyed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 6

podcast.title: Close Relationship with Funk
podcast.body: In many instances, disco was essentially funk re-branded, sharing similar musical foundations and often being "just funk by another name." "and then of course there was disco, which in many cases was really just funk by another name."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Give Up the Funk Edition Part 2

podcast.title: Club DJs as Hitmakers
podcast.body: In the early disco era (before 1974-1975), club DJs, not radio DJs, were primarily responsible for making songs hits. They controlled the atmosphere on the dance floor and dictated the music flow without taking requests. "The DJs in the clubs were the ones who made a song a hit, not the radio DJs. In these clubs, DJ was king."

srcs.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)

podcast.title: Club vs. Radio Singles
podcast.body: There was often a distinction between disco singles played in clubs, where DJs curated mixes to keep people dancing, and those played on the radio, aimed at attracting listeners for advertisers. Songs that succeeded in both realms were particularly notable. "there was often a difference between the disco singles that were played in clubs and the disco singles that were on the radio."

srcs.episode: Ep. 31 - The Spirit of '76 - Pop Music on America's Bicentennial

podcast.title: Complicated Relationship with Hip Hop
podcast.body: The relationship between disco and hip hop was complex, marked by both influence and rejection. Hip hop borrowed key techniques like the two-turntable method and the use of break beats, perfected by house DJs in discos. However, hip hop also emerged as a reaction against disco's polished, orchestral sound and its focus on production rather than the black artists who often created the music. Disco's "glitz and glamour" was seen as unrelatable to the realities of the Bronx, leading young artists to create their own "more real" music. "However, it is also true that the relationship between disco and hip hop is complicated."

srcs.episode: Ep. 6 - The 70s Roots of Hip Hop

podcast.title: Confrontation with Rock Music
podcast.body: The conflict surrounding disco began when it moved from underground clubs to mainstream radio, television, movies, and record stores. Rock music, which primarily served straight white men and took itself seriously in the 1970s, viewed disco's expansion as an affront to its established cultural space. "It is when disco moves from underground to radio, television, movies, your local tower records that the conflict begins because rock music took itself very seriously in the 1970s."

srcs.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)

podcast.title: Connection to Roller Skating Popularity
podcast.body: The rise in disco music in the 1970s shared a "happy marriage" with roller skating, particularly roller disco. Both phenomena were fueled by a similar "desire to escape" and provided feel-good moments for people, contributing to their widespread popularity among adults, not just children. "And certainly there is going to be a happy marriage between disco and roller skating in the form of roller disco."

srcs.episode: Ep. 36 - Na Na Na Na, Hey Hey Hey! 70s Music and Sports

podcast.title: Contemporary Perception
podcast.body: Today, disco is often merely regarded as "cheesy music from the past," a stark contrast to the fervent hatred it generated among rock fans in 1978. "Now today disco is merely cheesy music from the past, but if you were alive in 1978 and into rock there was nothing and I mean nothing you hated more than disco."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 6

podcast.title: Contributing Factor to Vinyl Decline
podcast.body: Disco was cited, along with the 1973 Arab Oil Embargo, as one of the primary factors that "killed" the vinyl record. "The things that killed vinyl was the 1973 Arab Oil embargo and disco."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Vinyl: Part 2

podcast.title: Contribution to Hip Hop
podcast.body: Disco was one of the key genres from which hip hop borrowed during its formative years. Though disco dominated the mainstream charts and clubs in the late 1970s, hip hop was developing by integrating elements from funk, soul, and disco. "It's going to borrow from funk and soul and disco and it is going to have a say."

srcs.episode: Ep. 22 - Power to the People - The Music of the Black Power Movement

podcast.title: DJ Influence on Hits
podcast.body: Manu Dibango's "Soul Makossa" (1972) is recognized as one of the earliest examples demonstrating the profound influence of DJs, rather than conventional radio, in creating disco hits and shaping the genre's sound. "This might be the very first song that showed the influence that DJs, not radio, were going to have over making disco hits."

srcs.episode: Ep. 33 - Zaire '74, Muhammad Ali, and The Rumble in the Jungle

podcast.title: Daft Punk's Integration
podcast.body: Disco elements, particularly "potent disco passages", were notably integrated into Daft Punk's "Discovery" album, initially leading to critical shock but later becoming a foundational aspect of modern music. "Teníamos esas pasas tan potentes en la música disco."

srcs.episode: Daft Punk - Interstella 5555

podcast.title: Disco Bubble Burst
podcast.body: The immense popularity and profitability of disco eventually came to an end as the "disco bubble finally burst." This decline, alongside the breakups and waning influence of major rock bands, prompted record executives to explore other emerging musical styles like New Wave. "the disco bubble finally burst, the record executives looked to this weird music and thought, let's see if we can tame it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 8

podcast.title: Dominance in Late 1970s
podcast.body: Disco emerged as the dominant sound in both R&B and Pop by the late 1970s, leading to varying degrees of adaptation success among vocalists who rose to prominence in the 1960s. "By the late 70s, both R&B and Pop had moved on to the sounds of disco."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Say a Little Prayer Edition Part 2

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Say a Little Prayer Edition Part 2

podcast.title: Dominance in Mid to Late 70s
podcast.body: Disco became a dominant musical genre in the mid to late 1970s. Casey Kasem adapted his on-air persona to match the upbeat nature of the music during this era, maintaining a sincere and engaging presence for listeners. "And by the time we get to the disco era of the mid to late 70s, he was upbeat like the music."

srcs.episode: Ep. 39 - American Top 40 - Keeping Our Feet on the Ground and Reaching for the Stars (Part 1)

podcast.title: Dominance in Mid-to-Late 70s
podcast.body: Disco exerted a significant "stranglehold" on the Billboard charts during the mid-to-late 1970s, as the demand for dance music and escapism increasingly became the dominant trend in popular music sales. "The desire for dance music dominates the pop charts."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: Dominance in the 1970s
podcast.body: Disco music significantly impacted the pop charts in the late 1970s, particularly exemplified by the success of the Bee Gees and the "Saturday Night Fever" soundtrack. "The Bee Gees were about to dominate the pop charts."

srcs.episode: Ep. 28 - Soundtracks of the 70s

podcast.title: Early Inclusive Environment
podcast.body: Before films like *Saturday Night Fever* brought disco into the mainstream, it was a vibrant dance music primarily for gay and Latin dance clubs in New York. It provided an inclusive environment for expression, where individuals could embrace their identity or an ideal self, a significant contrast to a time when same-sex dancing was often illegal. "It was a dance of expression, and it afforded an opportunity to not even necessarily be yourself, but I think be someone you would like to be if you were not at this club."

srcs.episode: Ep. 50 - The Travolta Trilogy

podcast.title: Early Influence (1970s)
podcast.body: Sinead O'Connor gravitated to disco music in her youth, alongside early punk, Bowie, Bob Marley, and Barbara Streisand, showing a diverse range of musical tastes. "Later it was Bowie and Bob Marley and Disco in early punk, and Barbara Streisand."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Remembering Sinead O'Connor

podcast.title: Early Influence on Mixing Techniques (Late 1970s)
podcast.body: In the late 1970s, some American funky and disco DJs began creating new songs by mixing rhythmic parts from various tracks. These experimental mixes were played in discotheques and became highly successful, leading to the circulation of pirated cassettes and eventually the commercialization of mixed records. "A finales de los años 70, algunos diges norteamericanos de fanque y disco empezaron a crear canciones mezclando partes rímpicas de varios temas para reproducirlos en discotecas, donde eran todo un éxito."

srcs.episode: Ritmo y Extorsión: Así Dominaron los Megamix los 90s

podcast.title: Economic Bubble and Collapse (Late 1970s)
podcast.body: Disco became a massive economic bubble for record labels in the late 1970s, generating "gazillions of dollars" until it popped, contributing to a severe recession and a free fall in record sales. "Then there was the disco problem. Through the late 70s, the record labels made gazillions of dollars pumping out disco records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Vinyl: Part 2

podcast.title: Emergence and Dominance
podcast.body: Disco began to emerge and gain prominence as a distinct genre around the mid-1970s, coinciding with the waning popularity of a specific "brand of soul" music. From 1975 to 1979, disco "ruled the charts and the clubs and the radio," becoming the prevailing sound of the era. "It is not a coincidence that as this brand of soul is fading out, disco was moving in."

srcs.episode: Ep. 22 - Power to the People - The Music of the Black Power Movement

podcast.title: End of Dominance
podcast.body: Chic's "Good Times," one of the last disco hits, ironically sparked the creation of "Rapper's Delight," the first mainstream hip hop record. This event signaled the eventual end of disco's dominance on the pop charts, as hip hop began its rise to prominence. "Good Times was the last hit record that Sheik ever had, and so I guess it's appropriate that it sparks one of the things that will signal an end to Disco's dominance on the pop charts, which is of course hip hop."

srcs.episode: Ep. 6 - The 70s Roots of Hip Hop

podcast.title: European Disco Characteristics
podcast.body: Unlike the pure, Afro-American-influenced disco popularized by artists like Gloria Gaynor, European disco did not penetrate the continent in the same way. Europe developed a distinct version of disco, featuring artists such as ABBA and Cerrone, with different influences, including a strong German component and less reliance on black music. "la música disco pura tal como la conocemos tan influenciada por Gloria Gaynor la música afroamericana no llegó a penetrar en Europa y tenían en Europa una versión un tanto distinta de lo que era la música disco."

srcs.episode: Grace Jones - Inicios de la Disco Queen

podcast.title: European Disco Electronic Foundation
podcast.body: European disco was less predominant and had fewer Afro-American influences compared to its US counterpart; its bases were largely drawn from European electronic music, making it much more electronic and rhythmically charged. "casi todas las bases de la música disco europea eran muy de la electrónica europea."

srcs.episode: De KRAFTWERK al TECHNO. Cómo se sentaron las bases del Techno

podcast.title: European Disco as Techno Pillar
podcast.body: The very electronic, strong rhythmic bases of European disco, exemplified by artists like Cerrone and Giorgio Moroder, constitute one of the grand pillars that founded techno music. "todas esas bases electrónicas tan duras que tenían la música disco aquí en Europa."

srcs.episode: De KRAFTWERK al TECHNO. Cómo se sentaron las bases del Techno

podcast.title: Evolution of Disco (1970s)
podcast.body: Disco music, which originated in the early 1970s, was initially heavily influenced by soul and Afro-American music. However, by the late 1970s, it began evolving, seeking new directions and incorporating more electronic and "discotec" elements. "la música disco que venía ya de la primera parte de los 70 era todavía muy influenciada del sól y de la música afroamericana y estaba hallándose a otroslares y estaba un poco ya perdiendo."

srcs.episode: Grace Jones - Inicios de la Disco Queen

podcast.title: Evolution: Philly Sound to Synthesizers
podcast.body: Disco music was not static; it evolved from the "Philly sound" (often characterized by strings) towards more synthesizer-heavy productions, exemplified by songs like Donna Summer's "I Feel Love." "It was evolving away from the philly sound of Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff for better or worse. If you don't know what I mean, just kind of think of disco with strings to synthesizers."

srcs.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)

podcast.title: Extended Mix Popularization
podcast.body: The "Love to Love You Baby" single and album were instrumental in reimagining disco as album-length music and significantly helped to popularize the concept of the extended mix, pushing the boundaries of traditional single lengths. "reimagining disco as album length music and helping to popularize the concept of the extended mix."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: The Queen of Disco Edition Part 1 (Encore)

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: The Queen of Disco Edition Part 1 (Encore)

podcast.title: Female Sexual Expression
podcast.body: The disco audience was particularly receptive to a new and bolder expression of female sexuality, with artists like Donna Summer becoming prominent figures in this movement. "The Disco audience welcomed a new boldness in the expression of female sexuality."

srcs.episode: Ep. 4 - Music of the 70s (Sexual) Revolution

podcast.title: First Disco Song ("Girl You Need A Change of Mind")
podcast.body: Many historians widely credit Eddie Kendricks' song "Girl You Need A Change of Mind," which he performed on the show "Soul Unlimited," as being the pioneering track of the disco genre. "He sang Girl You Need A Change of Mind, which many historians credit with being the first disco song."

srcs.episode: Ep. 47 - Dick Clark's Entertainment Empire

podcast.title: Fuel for a "Weary Nation"
podcast.body: The popularity of disco in 1976 and 1977 was partly fueled by a "weary nation," suggesting a desire for less politically charged or demanding music. "We were a weary nation in 1976, 1977, which was part of the disco fuel by the way."

srcs.episode: Ep. 29 - Every Little Thing is Gonna Be All Right - The Influence of 70s Reggae

podcast.title: Gamble & Huff as Architects
podcast.body: Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff are recognized as key architects of disco due to their innovative productions, particularly those that introduced elements like the "four-on-the-floor" beat, despite their later rejection of the genre. "Gamble and Huff rejected Disco later in the decade, but that does not change the fact that they were two of its architects."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: Height of the Disco Era (1970s)
podcast.body: The disco era reached its zenith during the 1970s, exemplified by the release of the movie "Thank God It's Friday" and the massive success of Donna Summer's song "Last Dance." "this is at the height of the disco era."

srcs.episode: Ep. 47 - Dick Clark's Entertainment Empire

podcast.title: Heresy for Punks
podcast.body: In 1978, a disco-influenced track by John Lydon, formerly the main face of punk, was considered an "absolute heresy" by many punk fans, as punk did not get along well with disco music. "Que John Leidon, que n' había sido la principal cara del punk unos meses atrás y cierra un tema disco, fue una heregía para muchos."

srcs.episode: La traición que salvó al punk. PiL

podcast.title: Hip Hop and Rap as Counter-Reaction
podcast.body: Many African Americans disliked disco, and their dissatisfaction contributed to the emergence of hip hop and rap, a new form of music focused less on production and more on the artist. "there were plenty of African Americans who did not like disco and their distaste for it will fuel the creation of hip hop and rap."

srcs.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)

podcast.title: Impact on Dancing
podcast.body: For many music fans, disco was seen as having "killed dancing dead," leading to a period where paying to dance in a dark room to overpriced beer and records played by a DJ was viewed negatively. However, memories of disco faded, and club dancing eventually became cool again, especially with the emergence of new music. "For many music fans, disco killed dancing dead."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 10

podcast.title: Impact on Live Music Venues
podcast.body: The rise of disco led to clubs replacing live music stages with DJ booths, as spinning records proved significantly cheaper than compensating live musicians. This shift caused widespread resentment among musicians and rock music enthusiasts. "Clubs that used to have live music replaced their stages with DJ booths, spinning records was far cheaper than paying musicians."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 6

podcast.title: Impact on Pop and R&B (Late 1970s)
podcast.body: Disco emerged around 1977 and "created a series of schisms" in both pop and R&B, contributing to the fragmentation of popular music. "Then disco hits, which created a series of schisms in both pop and R&B."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rock Snob

podcast.title: Impact on Remix Culture
podcast.body: Although disco "imploded by the beginning of the 80s," its influence on remix culture, particularly the 12-inch extended remix, endured. The genre's demand for continuous dance music led to innovations like extended mixes and the birth of the 12-inch single, which became crucial tools for DJs. "Even though disco had imploded by the beginning of the 80s, the 12 inch extended remix survived."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Remixes

podcast.title: Incorporation by Alaska y los Pegamoides
podcast.body: The band Alaska y los Pegamoides incorporated disco elements into their music, alongside New Wave and punk, as seen in their album "Grandes Éxitos." This fusion contributed to their mainstream appeal. "una colección de canciones New Wave, Punk y Estadisco."

srcs.episode: La España Siniestra ｜ La edad de oro del Postpunk y el Dark wave

podcast.title: Industry Dominance and Decline
podcast.body: Disco began to take hold in the mid-1970s, making it difficult for rock bands to find work as rock clubs closed. The genre gained significant power, with artists either temporarily adopting disco elements or establishing themselves purely as disco artists. By 1979, however, disco was already on its way off the radio. "Disco was taking over the music industry. But you could not make rock. I mean Van Halen was playing clubs and released their debut album in 1978. But you had to be like, well, Van Halen to get played in a rock club."

srcs.episode: Ep. 60 - One-Hit Wonders of the 70s

podcast.title: Industry Over-saturation and Crash
podcast.body: The record industry became excessively invested in disco, leading to the production of many "bad records" and an intense backlash. This over-saturation, culminating in events like the "Disco Demolition Night" in Chicago in summer 1979, caused the disco craze to crash and burn by 1980, sending the entire recorded music industry into a deep crisis. "There was too much disco and the backlash was intense."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 4: Alt-Dance

podcast.title: Influence of Funk Bass Lines
podcast.body: Disco hits by both white and Black performers, such as the Bee Gees' "Jive Talkin'" and Rose Royce's "Car Wash," were often built on popping funk bass lines, demonstrating funk's foundational role in the genre. "Like Jive Talking, Car Wash was built out of a popping funk bass line."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Give Up the Funk Edition Part 2

podcast.title: Influence on 2000s Alt Rock
podcast.body: Disco was one of the "million different types of dance influences" that artists in the 2000s integrated with alt rock sensibilities, demonstrating the genre's broad and fragmented approach to sound. "These acts blended alt rock sensibilities with a million different types of dance influences, from old school raves to disco to house to R&B to certain elements of hip hop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00s Part 4: Variety Returns

podcast.title: Inherently Happy Music
podcast.body: Disco is characterized as inherently happy music, serving as a respite from the often-negative news of the time. "still disco is inherently happy music and it did provide a respite from the news which was often not good."

srcs.episode: Ep. 31 - The Spirit of '76 - Pop Music on America's Bicentennial

podcast.title: Lamentable and Repetitive Lyrics
podcast.body: Disco music often featured truly lamentable lyrics, frequently repeating the same phrase over and over. This aspect is highlighted to counter the argument that only Trap music suffers from a lack of lyrical depth or sophistication. "tenemos letras de la música disco verdaderamente lamentables que la vez es lo único que hacen es repetir la misma frase una y otra vez."

srcs.episode: EL TRAP SÍ ES MÚSICA. (Aunque a lo mejor no te guste)

podcast.title: Late 70s Sound
podcast.body: In the late 1970s, disco music was ubiquitous, characterized by its "baroque" and elaborate nature, featuring many mixed sounds. This complexity was later contrasted by the birth of techno and house music in the early 80s.

srcs.episode: Daft Punk: Como el Homework revolucionó la electrónica

podcast.title: Late 70s/Early 80s Bubble Burst
podcast.body: The "disco bubble" burst as the 1970s turned into the 1980s, contributing to the recorded music industry's worst downturn since the 1930s and prompting an industry shift towards cheaper-to-produce New Wave acts. "As the 70s turned into 80s, the disco bubble burst, sending the recorded music industry into its worst downturn since the 1930s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

podcast.title: Legal Restrictions on Same-Sex Dancing
podcast.body: In the 1960s, same-sex dancing was illegal for the queer community, meaning even the right to dance with a chosen partner was questioned, creating a need for safe spaces like early disco clubs. "Remember that for the queer community in the 60s, it was not just same sex sex that was illegal. That was also true for same sex dancing."

srcs.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)

podcast.title: Mainstream Popularization and Downfall
podcast.body: While *Saturday Night Fever* undoubtedly introduced disco to a wider audience and contributed to its cultural significance, it also paradoxically led to the genre's over-saturation. This extensive exposure, in turn, contributed to disco's eventual decline in mainstream popularity. "And as Saturday Night Fever ultimately leads to the over saturation of disco and does contribute to its downfall and popularity."

srcs.episode: Ep. 50 - The Travolta Trilogy

podcast.title: Mid-1970s Profitability
podcast.body: In the mid-1970s, disco was a massively profitable genre, generating millions of dollars and sweeping the world. Its financial success contributed to major record labels' initial disinterest in the nascent punk rock scene. "And there was millions more coming from disco."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 8

podcast.title: Mini-Moog's Prominence
podcast.body: The Mini-Moog synthesizer is considered the most famous synth in history due to its extensive use across a wide array of genres, including disco. Its unique sounds and portability made it highly desirable for musicians seeking innovative textures. "I think it's the most famous synth in history given how much it was used in rock, pop, disco, funk, R&B, and jazz."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock's Most Iconic Instruments

podcast.title: Monotony and Economic Disparity
podcast.body: Despite its positive aspects, disco was also perceived as monotonous and dull. The stark contrast between the decadent, fun-seeking "rich and beautiful people" in exclusive disco clubs and the wider population struggling with a global recession and over 20% interest rates in the late 1970s fueled a significant backlash. "And everyone else was worrying about paying the mortgage with interest rates over 20%."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 4: Alt-Dance

podcast.title: Motown's Impact on 1960s Disco
podcast.body: Disco music from the 1960s was among the genres extensively covered by Motown Records, which contributed significantly to the landscape of black music during that era. "la música disco de los años 60."

srcs.episode: We are the world

podcast.title: One-Hit Wonders
podcast.body: One-hit wonders appeared across the Disco genre in the 1970s. "We saw them in Glamrock, Disco, Soft Rock, Punk."

srcs.episode: Ep. 60 - One-Hit Wonders of the 70s

podcast.title: Origin of Disco Beat
podcast.body: Session drummer Earl Young is credited with creating the foundational disco beat on Harold Melvin & The Blue Notes' "The Love I Lost." He achieved this by speeding up the track and introducing a "four-on-the-floor" rhythm with the bass drum on every beat, coupled with a prominent high-hat cymbal. "Earl Young created the disco beat."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: Outlet for the Disenfranchised
podcast.body: Bruce Schulman, a history professor at Boston University, described disco as "an outlet for the disenfranchised," serving as a refuge for gay, Latin, and African American people who felt uncomfortable or unwelcome in other public spaces in the early 1970s. "Bruce Schulman, a history professor at Boston University and the author of a book on 70s culture said that disco was and I quote an outlet for the disenfranchised."

srcs.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)

podcast.title: Perception of Emptiness
podcast.body: At the end of the 1970s, disco was widely perceived by "cool" people as lightweight, vacuous, and empty, in contrast to the perceived authenticity and intellectualism of New Wave. "there was disco, which no cool person ever admitted to liking. It was just vacuism empty."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

podcast.title: Pioneering Keyboard Use
podcast.body: Donna Summer's 1977 disco song "I Feel Love," produced by Giorgio Moroder, was hugely influential in its innovative use of new keyboards, featuring a mechanical beat and programmed synthesizer pulse that sounded exceptionally high-tech for its time. "Yes, it's done summer and yes, it's a disco song. I feel love from 1977, produced by an Italian guy named Georgioma Rotor. Hugely influential approach to the use of these new keyboards. The technology behind that track grabbed the attention of a lot of people, including a lot of disco haters, the mechanical beat, the programmed synthesizer pulse. In 1977, nothing, and I mean absolutely nothing sounded this high tech and this futuristic."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of New Wave through Techno-Pop

podcast.title: Post-Fad Evolution and Legacy
podcast.body: While the disco "fad" ended by 1980 due to fatigue and new trends like "Urban Cowboy," the music itself never truly died. Its DNA evolved into new wave in the 1980s and remains firmly present in hip hop and modern dance music. Disco clubs in cities like Wichita, Kansas City, and Omaha closed by 1984. "Disco never died though. The Fad did. Disco fatigue was real by 1980."

srcs.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)

podcast.title: Pre-Disco Era Defined
podcast.body: Music journalist Vince Letty referred to a "pre-disco era" for music existing before the "disco" label was commonly used and before major phenomena like Donna Summer's rise or "Saturday Night Fever." "Vincileti, the music journalist who was without a doubt, the very first to take disco seriously refers to a predisco era."

srcs.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)

podcast.title: Pure Good Time Music
podcast.body: Disco emerged as "pure good time music" following the economic recovery after the 1970s oil crisis. "More striking though was disco, which was pure good time music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: Purpose and Cultural Significance
podcast.body: At its core, disco was dance music focused on "forgetting your problems and dancing." Beyond being popular dance music, it held significant cultural importance for communities like the gay community, offering spaces for expression and celebration. "Yes, it was more than that to the gay community, of course. But at its heart, it is dance music."

srcs.episode: Ep. 22 - Power to the People - The Music of the Black Power Movement

podcast.title: R&B Expansion
podcast.body: Disco emerged as an expansion of R&B's main sounds post-1978, alongside the rapid mutation of funk and soul. "R&B's main sounds, which included fun console, began mutating even faster, expanding to include disco, and within a year, hip hop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

podcast.title: Racism in Backlash
podcast.body: The fact that disco was created by and primarily attracted non-white and/or non-straight individuals was a significant factor fueling racist backlash against the genre. "it is not a coincidence that by the mid 1970s rock music was the domain of white straight people, especially men."

srcs.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)

podcast.title: Regional Scenes
podcast.body: In the early period, disco music popularity was very regional, with different songs being "hot" in clubs in cities like Chicago, Philadelphia, or Los Angeles. "music that was hot in a club in Chicago might be different from music that was like hot in Philadelphia or Los Angeles. It was very regional at that time."

srcs.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)

podcast.title: Rehabilitation as Revivalist Notion
podcast.body: Disco, despite its past reception, has "somehow been rehabilitated" and is now included among the various revivalist trends. "even disco has somehow been rehabilitated."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

podcast.title: Resurgence in Chicago House
podcast.body: In Chicago, disco music was resisting its decline and evolved into House music. Instead of using traditional bands, House artists embraced rhythm machines and samples to recreate the disco sound. "El House de Chicago... es una evolución de la música disco, la cual se estaba resistiendo a morir en la ciudad."

srcs.episode: Cómo Detroit Reinventó la Música Electrónica ｜ Pioneros del Techno

podcast.title: Rise During Hard Times
podcast.body: A theory suggests dance music, including disco, gains popularity during or after difficult periods, providing an escape from reality. This partially explains the disco explosion that began in the mid-1970s, though it's acknowledged that disco's role in gay liberation in the 1970s is also significant. "there's a theory that dance music is most popular during hard times or on the heels of hard times the idea being a course that we need an escape from reality."

srcs.episode: Ep. 31 - The Spirit of '76 - Pop Music on America's Bicentennial

podcast.title: Rise in 1970s
podcast.body: Disco emerged and "took over" the music scene in the second half of the 1970s, marking a shift from the ballad-heavy trends of the decade's earlier years. "especially its first half before disco took over."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Song(s) of the Summer Edition Part 2

podcast.title: Rise in the 1970s
podcast.body: Disco music became a prominent genre in the 1970s, a development linked to a broader cultural sentiment where many Americans, including activists, sought to withdraw and disengage from societal pressures. "hence dance music and disco."

srcs.episode: Ep. 43 - Music and The Kent State Massacre of May 4, 1970

podcast.title: Rise of 12-inch Single and Remix (1970s)
podcast.body: With the rise of disco and early DJ culture in the 1970s, the 12-inch single and the extended remix emerged as new formats. "And with disco in the rise of early DJ culture came the 12-inch single and the extended remix."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Vinyl: Part 2

podcast.title: Rock Declared Dead During Disco Era (Late 1970s)
podcast.body: Rock music was among the many times it was declared dead during the late 1970s, a period when disco music was particularly prevalent and popular. This reflects a recurring pattern where new genres are seen as replacing and killing off established ones. "Rock was declared dead again in the early 70s, the late 70s during disco, the middle 80s, the middle 90s, and again and again and again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The More Things Change Part 2

podcast.title: Shift from Message Music to Escapism
podcast.body: As the 1970s progressed into the disco era, there was a notable decline in public demand for "message music," with a preference shifting towards songs offering escapism, which impacted the commercial viability of politically charged tracks. "There was less demand for message music. There was more demand for escapism."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: Shift to Exclusivity
podcast.body: The inclusive nature of early disco began to change in the late 1970s with the rise of clubs like Studio 54. These venues transformed disco into an exclusive environment that placed a primary focus on appearance rather than pure expression, diverging from its underground origins. "Disco was an inclusive environment until clubs like Studio 54 came along late in the 70s and ruined all that and made it instead an exclusive environment that was solely focused on how you looked."

srcs.episode: Ep. 50 - The Travolta Trilogy

podcast.title: Source for Early Hip Hop Samples
podcast.body: Disco music was a key genre utilized by early hip hop producers for sampling. They would extract brief musical fragments from disco records, along with soul and funk, to form repetitive loops that underpinned early hip hop instrumentals. "se basaba en coger de canciones que ya existían, principalmente del sol, del fankey, del musical disco."

podcast.title: Ubiquity and Backlash (Late 1970s)
podcast.body: In the late 1970s, disco music was ubiquitous, especially on the radio, and its cultural dominance lasted for a couple of years, notably aiding the liberation of gay and certain minority groups. However, it also became associated with decadence, drugs, sex, and exclusive clubs that often excluded those not considered "pretty enough" or "dressed in the right high end clothes." "disco was so huge that it drove the culture for a couple of years."
